stimulus:
Text 1
Critics have long read Ines Varga's 1958 novel *The Last Speakers*, about a linguist transcribing a vanishing coastal dialect, as an elegy. The linguist's notebooks fill as the village empties, and the book closes as she records the dialect's last fluent speaker. The novel, critics conclude, mourns a language already lost.

Text 2
Varga's novel does close with that recording. But just before it, the linguist plays her tapes for village children, who mimic the phrases, garble them, and reuse them in their games. Varga presents the language not as dead but as changing hands.
choices: The novel treats the coastal dialect as a language that has already died.
The novel closes as the linguist records the dialect's last fluent speaker.
The children's games show the dialect surviving in an altered form.
The filling notebooks mirror the gradual emptying of the coastal village.
explanation: Text 1 says the book 'closes as she records the dialect's last fluent speaker,' and Text 2 opens by granting it: 'Varga's novel does close with that recording.' Text 2 parts ways with Text 1 only after that concession, so the ending itself is what both authors share.

A.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, and Text 2 rejects it outright: Varga presents the language 'not as dead but as changing hands.' You picked a claim that only one author holds.

C.why: This is Text 2's reading. Text 1 never mentions the children and calls the language 'already lost,' so Author 1 would not accept this.

D.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a reasonable reading of the novel's imagery, and Text 1 mentions it, but Text 2 never takes it up. You read the novel yourself instead of finding the point the two critics share.

Literary historians have generally treated *Loom Songs* (1847), a collection by mill weaver Hannah Pell, as a record of factory hardship. Its poems dwell on clattering power looms, lint-choked air, and fourteen-hour shifts; scholars therefore value it chiefly as documentary evidence of early textile labor.

Text 2
Pell's poems do catalogue the miseries of the mill floor. Yet reading them only as documents overlooks their craft: many stanzas follow the back-and-forth rhythm of a shuttle, so that the verse itself imitates weaving. Pell was a deliberate artist, not merely a witness.
choices: Loom Songs is valuable chiefly as evidence about early textile labor.
Pell patterned the rhythm of many stanzas on a shuttle's motion.
Pell wrote her poems mainly to win shorter shifts for mill weavers.
Pell's poems depict the harsh conditions of work in textile mills.
explanation: Text 1 says the poems 'dwell on' looms, lint-choked air, and long shifts. Text 2 concedes this ('Pell's poems do catalogue the miseries of the mill floor') before turning to the poems' craft. The harsh conditions they depict are what both authors share.

A.why: This is Text 1's position, and Text 2 is written to challenge it: reading the poems 'only as documents overlooks their craft.' Author 2 would not agree.

B.why: This is Text 2's new observation. Text 1 treats the poems purely as documentary evidence and says nothing about their rhythm, so you can't credit it to Author 1.

C.why: This is the subtype's trap. Given the poems' subject, it's a plausible guess about Pell, but neither critic says she wrote to campaign for reform. You reasoned from the poems' content instead of from what the critics argue.

The burning coal represents ancient sunlight being returned as warmth.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 rejects it directly: 'The poem concerns not loss but energy returning to use.'

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. It's a vivid reading of the quoted image, but neither critic interprets the 'green hand' this way. You read the poem yourself instead of looking for what the critics share.

stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is adapted from Martha Greaves's 1861 novel The Thorne Inheritance. A surgeon is inoculating Mrs. Thorne's son against smallpox.
Mrs. Thorne watched the surgeon lay the infected thread in the shallow cut on her son's arm. The village called it tempting Providence. Still she held the boy steady, reasoning that a small fever, chosen, was kinder than a great one left to chance.

Text 2
Critics often read Greaves's inoculation scenes as simple celebrations of medical progress. The novel certainly admires the procedure, but its mothers do not trust science blindly. They weigh one harm against another, and the book's real subject is the burden of choosing a lesser danger.
choices: Mrs. Thorne knowingly accepts a smaller danger to protect her son from a greater one.
The scene mainly shows how skillfully the surgeon carries out a delicate procedure.
The novel is best read as a straightforward celebration of medical progress.
The novel finally condemns inoculation as a risk that no parent should take.
explanation: Start with the critic's thesis in Text 2: the novel is about the burden of choosing a lesser danger. Then find the feature in Text 1 that fits it: Mrs. Thorne reasons that 'a small fever, chosen, was kinder than a great one left to chance.' The excerpt shows her making exactly the weighing the critic describes, so both authors would agree with this statement.

B.why: You read the excerpt on its own terms and fixed on the surgeon's action, which is vividly described. The critic, though, cares about the mother's choice, not the surgeon's technique, and Text 1 never says the procedure is skillful. Neither author supports this as the scene's main point.

C.why: This is the common reading that Text 2 brings up only to push back on. The critic grants that the novel admires inoculation but says its real subject is the burden of choosing harm. The critic would reject calling the novel a 'straightforward' celebration.

D.why: You went too far with the villagers' 'tempting Providence.' Mrs. Thorne goes ahead with the inoculation anyway, and the critic says outright that the novel admires the procedure. Neither text says the novel condemns it.

stimulus:
Text 1
The following text is from Agnes Tolliver's 1894 poem "Heron at Low Water."
The heron stands where the shallows thin,
A gray thought in the gray of the morning,
Patient as stone till the fish slides in—
Then the strike, and no warning.

Text 2
Tolliver's heron is usually taken as a portrait of serenity, a bird at rest in a quiet dawn. That calm is real, but it is never idle. Each still line leans toward the closing strike, so that the bird's patience becomes a kind of menace and its waiting turns out to be the hunt itself.
choices: The heron's stillness is directed toward a sudden act of catching prey.
The poem's main interest is the gray color shared by the bird and dawn.
The heron is best understood as a symbol of untroubled, restful peace.
The poem shows that Tolliver admired hunting birds above all others.
explanation: The critic's thesis in Text 2 is that the heron's calm is 'never idle': its patience leads to the strike and is part of the hunt. Text 1 shows this. The bird is 'patient as stone till the fish slides in— / Then the strike.' Both texts tie the heron's stillness to a sudden attack on prey, so both authors would agree.

B.why: This is the bait: you paraphrased a striking image from the poem ('a gray thought in the gray of the morning') instead of reading through the critic's lens. Text 2 never mentions color, and the poem uses the gray image as one detail, not its main interest.

C.why: This is the usual reading that Text 2 corrects. The critic grants that the calm is real but argues it is 'never idle' and amounts to 'a kind of menace,' so the critic would not accept 'untroubled' peace.

D.why: Neither text compares herons with other birds or says what Tolliver preferred. You stretched one poem about one heron into a claim about the poet's views on all birds.

The following text is adapted from Ada Marlow's 1909 poem "Shuttle Song."
My shuttle runs like a swallow, / back and over, back and over; / the cloth grows under my hands / as a meadow greens in April. / Twelve strokes, and the bell; / twelve strokes, and the bell.

"Shuttle Song" is often anthologized as a cheerful hymn to the loom, and its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness. Yet Marlow closes on a counted refrain tied to the mill bell. Beneath the borrowed countryside, the poem records labor measured out by someone else's clock.

explanation: Text 1 compares the shuttle to a swallow and the growing cloth to a meadow in April. Text 2 grants exactly this ('its swallows and meadows do lend it a pastoral sweetness') before it turns to the bell. Both authors accept that the poem uses countryside imagery for the work.

A.why: The critic finds the regimentation 'beneath' the imagery, which means it is hidden, not openly protested. The poem itself never complains.

C.why: Text 2 names this as the common reading and then disputes it, arguing that the bell refrain undercuts the cheer.

D.why: This is your own reading of the imagery, and the critic would not accept it. Text 2 argues that the sweetness hides labor controlled by 'someone else's clock.'

She is brave, certainly, but notice what actually moves Mrs. Hart: not the doctor's tables, which she ignores, but the sight of another person accepting the risk first. A.why: You stretched the critic's 'more than data' into 'no part at all.' Text 2 ranks trust above evidence. It does not throw evidence out.

B.why: Both texts say the reverse: Mrs. Hart draws her son closer while the tables are laid out, and the critic says she ignores them.

D.why: You read Text 1 your own way instead of through the critic's frame. Neither text calls her caution foolish, and the critic treats it as something to win over with trust.

Ilse Marrow's Garden Suite (1894) is a set of parlor confections: seven brief pieces of pleasant melody, written for amateur pianists to play after dinner. Nothing in them asks to be remembered the next morning, and their very brevity shows that Marrow aimed only to charm her listeners.

Granted, Marrow wrote the seven brief pieces of the Garden Suite for amateurs to play at home, and their melodies are easy to love. Yet nearly every piece ends on an unresolved chord, so the suite never comes to rest. That refusal quietly unsettles the very parlor the music was written to entertain.

The suite's only purpose is to charm and entertain its listeners.

Text 2 grants that the suite was written for amateurs, that it has appealing melodies, and that its pieces are short. Then it turns: the unresolved endings 'unsettle' the parlor, so charm is not the suite's only purpose. Text 2's critic would reject this statement, so it is the one both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have read Text 2's 'Yet' as rejecting everything before it. But Text 2 opens with 'Granted, Marrow wrote... for amateurs to play at home,' so it accepts this point outright. Both authors agree with it.

B.why: You may have reasoned that a critic who finds the suite unsettling can't think it is pleasant. That comes from your own reading of the music, not from Text 2. Text 2 calls the melodies 'easy to love' and argues that the unease comes from the endings, not the tunes.

D.why: Both texts describe the suite as 'seven brief pieces.' Text 2 never disputes the brevity. It disputes only what Text 1 concludes from it.

The poem's structure follows the cycle of the farming year.

Its main clause then rejects Text 1's central claim: the poem is 'less a manual than a lament.' The view that the poem's main purpose is instruction belongs to Text 1 alone, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

B.why: You may have assumed that a critic who calls the poem a lament must doubt its farming advice. Text 2 says outright that 'few would deny' the advice is accurate, so both authors accept this.

C.why: You may have dismissed this because Text 1 treats the village scenes as mere 'color.' The question asks only whether both authors would agree that the scenes are in the poem. They do agree, and in fact Text 2's whole reading depends on them.

D.why: Text 1 says the books 'follow the farming calendar month by month,' and Text 2 grants that the structure 'mirrors the agricultural calendar.' This is shared ground, not the point of disagreement.

Hana Ostrow's woodcut series Harbor Hours (1927) documents working life on the Baltic docks. Its twenty prints show stevedores hauling nets, coiling rope, and mending hulls, and every winch and cleat is cut with an engineer's precision. Ostrow plainly set out to preserve a faithful record of the dockworkers' labor.

Certainly the tackle in Harbor Hours is cut with exacting care, and the series never leaves the docks. But Ostrow printed each block repeatedly, carving more away between printings, so that in the final impressions the workers sink into solid black. Text 2 concedes the precise tackle and the dockside setting, and its own argument assumes the prints show workers. It then argues that the series records the labor's 'vanishing from view,' not the labor itself. A faithful record as Ostrow's chief aim is Text 1's view only, so it is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have focused on the image of workers sinking into black and decided Text 2 denies that the prints show labor. But figures can only disappear from prints that show them in the first place. Both authors agree that the series depicts dockworkers.

B.why: Text 2's 'Certainly the tackle... is cut with exacting care' grants this point. The 'But' that follows challenges what the series means, not how carefully it was cut.

C.why: Text 1 sets every print on the docks, and Text 2 says the series 'never leaves the docks.' Both authors agree on this.
